headings.title: Introduction to Descriptive Statistics and Central Tendency
headings.content:
Descriptive statistics allow researchers and healthcare practitioners to summarize large amounts of numerical data into manageable, meaningful summaries. When reviewing ward audits, patient satisfaction scores, or epidemiological reports, raw data is rarely useful on its own. Instead, summaries are needed to understand the typical observation within a group.

Central tendency refers to a single value that attempts to describe a set of data by identifying the central position within that dataset. Rather than looking at every individual patient's length of stay, a central tendency metric provides a single representative figure. The three most common measures utilized in nursing research and public health are the mean, the median, and the mode. Each metric approaches the 'center' differently, meaning the choice of statistic depends heavily on the shape of the data distribution and the scale used to measure the variable.

headings.title: The Mean: Calculation, Uses, and Limitations in Nursing Research
headings.content:
The mean, commonly known as the average, is calculated by summing all individual values in a dataset and dividing that sum by the total number of observations. It is heavily favored in parametric testing because it incorporates every single data point.

- **Calculation**: Sum of all values divided by the sample size ($n$).
- **Primary Advantage**: Highly sensitive to every value, making it mathematically stable for further statistical analysis.
- **Major Limitation**: Highly vulnerable to outliers. A single extreme value can severely skew the mean, pulling it away from where the majority of the data lies.

For example, if four patients on a post-surgical ward stay for 3, 4, 4, and 5 days, the mean stay is 4 days. However, if a fifth patient develops a severe complication and stays for 34 days, the mean length of stay jumps to 10 days. This higher average no longer accurately reflects the typical experience of the first four patients, illustrating why researchers must always inspect their data for extreme values before relying solely on the mean.

headings.title: The Median: Identifying the Middle Value in Skewed Data
headings.content:
The median is the exact middle value when a dataset is ordered numerically from lowest to highest. If a dataset has an odd number of observations, the median is the single middle number. If the number of observations is even, the median is calculated by taking the mean of the two middle numbers.

Unlike the mean, the median is non-parametric and remains resistant to extreme outliers. This property makes it the preferred measure of central tendency for skewed data distributions, such as household income, waiting times in emergency departments, or length of hospital stay. When a few patients experience exceptionally prolonged admissions, the median remains anchored near the true center of the majority of patient experiences, providing a much more realistic picture of typical ward dynamics.

headings.title: The Mode: Determining Most Frequent Clinical Observations
headings.content:
The mode represents the most frequently occurring value in a dataset. While mean and median require numerical data, the mode is unique because it can be used with categorical and nominal data. For instance, in a nursing assessment of blood types O, A, B, and AB within a cohort, the mode reveals which blood type is most prevalent.

A dataset can have a single mode (unimodal), two modes (bimodal), or multiple modes (multimodal). If every value appears only once, the dataset has no mode at all. In clinical practice, the mode is exceptionally useful for identifying the most common diagnosis, the most frequently prescribed drug class in a clinic, or the predominant triage category on a busy shift.

headings.title: Comparing Mean, Median, and Mode Across Different Data Distributions
headings.content:
The relationship between the mean, median, and mode changes predictably depending on the symmetry or asymmetry of the data distribution.

| Distribution Type | Relationship Among Metrics | Clinical Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Symmetrical (Normal)** | Mean $\approx$ Median $\approx$ Mode | Adult human body temperature readings |
| **Positively Skewed** | Mode $<$ Median $<$ Mean | Hospital charges or rare complication lengths of stay |
| **Negatively Skewed** | Mean $<$ Median $<$ Mode | Age at death in a modern high-income country |

In a positively skewed distribution, a long tail of high values pulls the mean upward, making it higher than the median. Conversely, in a negatively skewed distribution, a cluster of low values pulls the mean downward. Recognizing these relationships allows nurses to critically evaluate published research and spot when an author might be masking skewed data behind a misleading mean.

headings.title: Selecting the Appropriate Measure of Central Tendency Based on Scale of Measurement
headings.content:
Choosing the correct measure of central tendency is dictated strictly by the level of measurement of the data: nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio.

- **Nominal Scale**: Data classified into unordered categories (e.g., gender, blood type, ethnicity). Only the **mode** can be used.
- **Ordinal Scale**: Data placed in a ranked order, but intervals between ranks are unequal (e.g., pain scales like mild/moderate/severe, patient satisfaction ratings). The **median** and mode are appropriate.
- **Interval and Ratio Scales**: Numerical data with equal intervals and a true zero (for ratio). All three measures—**mean**, **median**, and **mode**—can be calculated, though the mean is generally preferred if the data is normally distributed.

Selecting an inappropriate measure—such as calculating the mean pain score on a verbal rating scale—is a frequent statistical error in clinical literature. Pain scores represent ordinal ranks, meaning an average score of 2.3 holds no mathematical interpretation in patient care.
